This city represents a community. Each building may look simple from the outside, but there are many different stories inside. The building in the centre represents me.
Daniel Heath Justice · "How do we learn to live together?"
Every person carries experiences that cannot be understood from the outside alone.
Childhood Memories

When I was younger, my whole family lived together, but as I got older, there was a time when I lived mostly with my father. Because he often worked late, I spent a lot of time by myself. From the outside, that might have seemed like freedom, but it also meant that my daily habits became unhealthy. I stayed up too late, played games for too long, and did not always take care of myself properly.

One memory that stayed with me was when my father came home late from work and caught me playing video games all night. He was very upset, and at the time, I mostly felt scared and embarrassed. Later, I understood why that moment mattered. It was not only about playing games. It helped me realize that the way I live affects not only me, but also the people who care about me. That experience taught me that responsibility is connected to family, and that improving myself can also help the people around me feel happier and less worried.

Why We Moved

People may know that I moved from Korea to Canada, but they may not know why my family made that decision. There were several reasons, but one of the main reasons was that my older brother had a very difficult experience in the Korean school system and struggled to feel accepted there. My family believed that moving to Canada could give him a chance to start again in a different environment.

Even though the decision was mainly focused on my brother, it completely affected my life as well. I had to leave my friends, adjust to a new country, and learn how to express myself in English. Looking back, I realize that a decision made because of one family member can shape the lives of everyone in the family.

Language

Sometimes people may think I am quiet, speaking in English has not always been easy for me. There have been many times when I knew what I wanted to say but needed more time to express it clearly.

Learning to communicate in a different language has made me more patient with myself. It has also reminded me that people may have thoughts, feelings, and ideas that they cannot easily show from the outside. Someone who seems quiet may still have a lot to say.

— 09 / 14

— 10 / 14

Friends and Community

Moving to Canada changed the way I thought about community. I lost daily contact with many of my friends in Korea and had to build new friendships in Canada.

This experience taught me that belonging can change over time. Some relationships may become less active when people are far apart, but that does not mean they stop mattering. I also learned that my new communities have became crucial without replacing the old ones. Because of this, I now understand that a person can feel connected to more than one place and more than one group of people.

— 12 / 14
Golf tryout with Kyle. He showed me how to swing. I was starting to feel less alone.
— 13 / 14
Mr. Guest passed away this week. I wore black every day. It was the only thing I knew how to do.
— 14 / 14
The day of my storytelling presentation. I have never been more nervous in my life.
Final Reflection
My artifact points to the question "How do we learn to live together?" because every person carries experiences that cannot be understood from the outside alone. The buildings in my cityscape may look similar from the street, but each one holds different stories, just as the people we live alongside carry histories we may never see. The different parts of my building show memories about my childhood, moving to Canada, learning English, and building new communities, which are all parts of me that people would not fully understand just by looking at me. This idea connects directly to Medicine Walk. Franklin only begins to truly understand Eldon after listening to stories he had never heard before. Living together requires more than sharing the same space. It requires a willingness to look beyond the surface, listen carefully, and recognize that every person is more than what we first see.
